issues.description: Cycle-detection comment claims `s.stack[0:]` was reset but new code now relies solely on deferred cleanup
issues.detail: Previously `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` (a no-op anyway) was at the top of Sort and `clear(s.state)` ran on entry. The new code moves cleanup entirely into the deferred function at the end. If `yield` panics on the consumer side, the deferred clear still runs — good. But if the caller obtains the `iter.Seq` and never iterates it (or stops before the first call), the defer doesn't run because the closure body has not started; the next Sort call inherits stale state. The previous version handled this by clearing on entry. Worth either clearing on entry too, or documenting that an unstarted Seq leaves state dirty.

The replacement comment at the DFS loop reads 'whether this node has been visisted and if its the first or second visit'. Two errors: 'visisted' should be 'visited', and 'if its' should be 'if it's'. Minor but the PR is explicitly touching the comment, so fixing it now is free.

issues.description: Collapsing `working` and `walking` into a single `walking` state loses a semantic distinction
issues.detail: The original three-state machine (unsorted/working/walking/sorted) distinguished 'currently descending into children' (working) from 'returned from children, on the stack pending finalize' (walking). After this PR they are the same state. The `push` function's `case walking` branch (which looks the node up in the stack to detect a cycle) now fires for both descent and ascent phases. This appears correct because a node in either phase is still on the stack, but the conceptual clarity is reduced. Confirm with tests that cycle detection still triggers in the same situations.

issues.description: `s.state[k] = sorted` now only runs when `state != sorted`
issues.detail: Previously the assignment ran unconditionally after the pop. Now it only runs in the `state != sorted` branch. This is logically equivalent (the only case where it differed was when `state` was already `sorted`, in which case writing `sorted` again was a no-op), but worth a one-line code comment or tested with a sorted-revisit case to ensure nothing relied on the unconditional write.

issues.description: `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` removal — note that the original was a no-op
issues.detail: The removed line `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` was equivalent to `s.stack = s.stack` and did not truncate length. So the original code never actually reset the stack between Sort calls; it relied on the loop running to completion (len==0 at end) for that. The new defer with `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` and `clear(s.stack)` is a real fix, addressing the case where iteration is abandoned mid-walk via `yield` returning false. Good fix; commit message could be clearer that this corrects a latent bug, not just refactors.

issues.description: `clear(s.stack)` before `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` is defensive but technically redundant for GC of slice elements only
issues.detail: `clear(s.stack)` zeros the elements so any pointer references in Node values become eligible for GC; then `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` truncates length. Order matters and is correct here. Worth a brief comment that the clear is to avoid leaking references when Node holds pointers.

dissents.topic: Whether cleanup belongs at function entry or via defer

positions.position: Cleanup-on-exit is sufficient and avoids redundant work; defer guarantees cleanup even on early yield-return. The Sort method only sets up state inside the returned closure, so cleanup must happen inside the closure too.

Clear on both entry and exit. If the caller obtains the Seq and discards it without iterating, the deferred cleanup never runs and the next Sort inherits stale state. Defensive cleanup on entry costs little and removes a sharp edge.

dissents.topic: Whether collapsing working+walking is a simplification or a loss of information

positions.position: Three states were one more than necessary; the algorithm only needs unsorted/in-progress/sorted. The rename to walking and removal of working tightens the state machine.
The two-phase distinction (descending vs ascending) is a common DFS idiom and may be useful for future features like reporting cycle paths. Keeping the distinction has zero runtime cost.

review.summary: The PR correctly fixes a real bug: the previous `s.stack = s.stack[0:]` was a no-op and stack/state weren't reliably reset when iteration was abandoned mid-walk. The new `defer` block with `clear(s.state)`, `clear(s.stack)`, and `s.stack = s.stack[:0]` properly handles early-exit cleanup. However, cleanup now only happens on exit of the iterator closure — if a caller obtains the `iter.Seq` and never starts iterating (or the previous run panicked before the defer was registered), stale state can leak into the next call; consider also clearing on entry. Two introduced comment typos ('visisted', 'if its') should be fixed since the PR is touching those lines. The state-machine collapse from working/walking to a single walking state is logically equivalent given current usage but trades a small amount of semantic clarity for simplicity. No P0 blockers.
